PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_TITLE: Start Your Korean Journey with a Short-Term Study Abroad Program
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_SUBTITLE_1: 📌 Benefits of a Short-Term Language Program
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_1_1: Regular language courses at university-affiliated institutes typically last around 10 weeks (3 months), and even at private schools, a minimum duration of one month is often required. This makes it difficult for working professionals or students to commit to long-term study abroad.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_1_2: However, if you're learning Korean, the desire to experience studying in Korea naturally grows. Language learning goes far beyond memorizing vocabulary — it's about living the language in its cultural context. A short-term language program is the ideal choice for learners looking for a meaningful experience without the long-term commitment.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_1_3: Many short-term programs do not require a visa, making them accessible and easy to join—just like taking a trip with an educational twist.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_2: Korean requires a strong foundation, and early learning should be accurate, focused and well-structured. For beginners who may find long-term programs overwhelming, short-term course is a perfect starting point.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_SUBTITLE_3: 🧑‍🎓 Valuable for Upper-Beginners and Intermediate Learners
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_3: If you've passed the beginner stage, staying in Korea even for a few weeks allows you to observe how locals think, speak, and behave—an experience that enhances both language skills and cultural understanding.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_4: Short-term programs are not available year-round. They are generally scheduled during vacation seasons:
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_4_1: Main intake periods: Summer break, spring/winter holidays, year-end/New Year
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_CONTENT_4_4: Ultra-short courses: 1 week, 3 days, or 5 days (offered occasionally)
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_1_1: Spring break, summer vacation, year-end and New Year holidays, etc.
PROGRAM_MODAL_SHORT_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_2_1: Spring break, summer vacation, autumn, year-end and New Year holidays, etc.
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_TITLE: Build a Strong Foundation with Our Long-Term Language Program
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_1_1: A long-term language program means studying at an official university-affiliated language institute in Korea for one or more semesters. Each semester lasts about 10 weeks (around 3 months), and you can continue for as many semesters as you like.
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_1_2: After a placement test, you will join a structured curriculum focused on grammar, listening, speaking, and writing, using standardized textbooks and balanced learning methods.
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_2: Language centers typically operate on a quarterly schedule, with each term lasting around 10 weeks. Students study 4–5 days a week: about 4 hours a day at university institutes and about 3 hours at language schools. After each level, you move up to the next tier.
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_3: You can achieve strong fluency, cultural immersion, and prepare for academic or professional goals like TOPIK certification or entering a Korean university.
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_4: For a long-term stay in Korea, you'll need to apply for a D-4 visa (language training visa). Most schools request the following:
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_4_3: Proof of last education (high school diploma or higher)
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_CONTENT_4_4: Proof of financial means (bank balance certificate)
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_1_1: 4 times a year (start of each semester in spring, summer, autumn, winter)
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_2_1: 12 times a year (classes start every month)
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_2_5: About 3 hours a day, from 10:00 (afternoon classes at some schools)
PROGRAM_MODAL_LONG_TERM_TABLE_VALUE_2_6: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri (4 days a week)

FAQ_DESCRIPTION: Answers to the questions we hear most often about studying Korean in Korea.
FAQ_Q1: Do I need to speak Korean before I join?
FAQ_A1: No. University language institutes teach Levels 1 to 6, so complete beginners start at Level 1. If you can already read Hangul, starting in Korea early is often more effective than spending more time on self-study at home. Students who have studied before take a placement test (written, speaking and listening) to find the right class.
FAQ_Q2: What is the difference between the short-term and long-term programs?
FAQ_A2: Short-term programs run during school holidays (spring, summer and winter/year-end). University courses usually last 3 weeks and language-school courses 1–2 weeks, often with cultural activities in the afternoons. The long-term program is the regular course at a university language institute: one semester lasts 10 weeks (about 3 months, around 200 class hours), with four intakes a year in spring, summer, autumn and winter. You can enroll for one semester or several.
FAQ_A3: Short-term programs do not require a student visa. For the long-term program, a single semester can usually be done without a visa if your nationality allows a visa-free stay of that length. For two or more semesters you need a D-4-1 (general training) visa, which you apply for at a Korean embassy or consulate using the admission letter. If your country has a working holiday agreement with Korea, an H-1 visa is another option for language schools, but it can only be issued once. Visa-free rules differ by nationality, so please check yours or ask us.
FAQ_Q4: How does the application work, and what documents do I need?
FAQ_A4: Once your plan is set, we send you a guide listing the exact documents and deadlines for your school. Typically this includes a photo, a certificate of graduation or enrollment, a copy of your passport and, for some schools, an essay. More and more schools also ask for proof of your highest level of education. We submit the application and pay the tuition to the school on your behalf, and the admission letter usually arrives 3–4 weeks later.
FAQ_Q5: Where will I live in Korea?
FAQ_A5: Most students live in a goshitel (also called goshiwon): a small, furnished private room with a shared kitchen, free Wi-Fi and utilities included, usually on monthly contracts. The rooms we arrange have their own toilet and shower. Other options include university dormitories (affordable and close to campus, but limited in Seoul and often only for one or two semesters), share houses, guesthouses for short stays, and studios or officetels for longer stays. We usually arrange accommodation one semester at a time.
FAQ_Q6: What does a typical class schedule look like?
FAQ_A6: At university language institutes, classes run Monday to Friday for 4 hours a day, usually from 9:00 to 13:00. Many institutes also run afternoon classes (for example 13:30–17:30), assigned by level or class size. Classes have about 10–15 students. With homework and review, you study Korean every day, around 200 class hours per semester. Language schools usually teach about 3 hours a day (for example 10:00–12:50) in smaller classes of about 5–10 students. The plan builder shows the class times for each school.
FAQ_Q7: Can I work part-time while studying?
FAQ_A7: With a D-4-1 visa, you can apply for permission to work part-time after six months of stay in Korea. This is not possible if you entered Korea without a visa.
FAQ_Q8: I want to study at a Korean university. Should I attend a language institute first?
FAQ_A8: Yes, we recommend it. University lectures, presentations and reports are all in Korean, and even with TOPIK Level 3 or 4 many students find it hard to keep up. Studying at a language institute first helps you get used to real-life Korean. Reaching an advanced TOPIK level before enrolling can also qualify you for larger scholarships, which can lower your overall costs.
FAQ_Q9: Can I get a refund if I cancel?
FAQ_A9: If you cancel before a semester starts, most schools refund almost the full tuition for that semester, depending on each school's rules. This makes enrolling for several semesters from the start a low-risk choice.
FAQ_A10: Book a free consultation using the contact form or email us at contact@aah.education. We will talk about your goals, current Korean level, preferred dates and budget, then recommend schools and accommodation. Once you are happy with the plan, we take care of the application, tuition payment, accommodation booking and visa guidance.
